title: How I Make $35k/Month With Other People's Content (Legally)
channel: Chris Koerner on The Koerner Office Podcast
promo_conflict: He promotes his own channel and newsletter funnel while presenting the business model; no external paid sponsorship is disclosed.

stated_problem.quote: The reason this is an opportunity is because Facebook has 2.1 billion daily active users, but they don't have enough creators publishing good content that these two billion people can actually consume on a daily basis.
stated_problem.speaker: Chris Koerner

idea.name: Add value to other people’s content on Facebook
idea.one_liner: Create original commentary or other added value around existing content, publish across social platforms, and earn platform ad revenue.
idea.customer: Social media audiences; Facebook pays eligible creators for content views.
idea.offer: Commentary, analysis, or other original additions to existing content, published as videos, images, carousels, or text.
idea.revenue_model: Platform monetization based on views; the speaker also describes paying an editor to produce posts that generated earnings.

key_quotes.quote: This is called fair use and it is protected legally if I am adding enough value or insight or adding commentary to make the video my own, original to me.
I give my spin on it, my take, how I would grow that business, how I would make it better
So I get paid about 25 cents per thousand views on my short form videos, which is pretty high.

claims.claim: He says he earns $10,000–$35,000 monthly profit from Facebook content and spends about three hours per week on it.
claims.quote: I make between $10,000 and $35,000 a month of profit on Facebook sharing content that is mostly not my own. I do this legally, ethically, and it only takes me about 3 hours per week.

claims.claim: He says Facebook has 2.1 billion daily active users and lacks enough creators publishing content for them.
claims.quote: The reason this is an opportunity is because Facebook has 2.1 billion daily active users, but they don't have enough creators publishing good content that these two billion people can actually consume on a daily basis.

claims.claim: He says over a quarter of the planet uses Facebook daily.
claims.quote: That's why over a quarter of the planet is using Facebook every single day.

claims.claim: He presents examples of earnings from his content over the preceding 90 days.
claims.quote: This is my Meta Business suite. And I'm just going to show you some examples of how much money my content has made over the last 90 days.

claims.claim: An original backyard bonfire video earned him $2,000.
claims.quote: This video about burning bonfires in my backyard made me $2,000.

claims.claim: He says about 90% of his other content is repurposed.
claims.quote: Now, that was an original video. I didn't repurpose anyone else's content there, but about 90% of this other content is mostly repurposed.

claims.claim: He started his social accounts from zero less than two years earlier.
claims.quote: I started all of these social accounts less than two years ago from zero. I did not even use my personal Facebook or Instagram accounts.

claims.claim: A photo post earned $150.
claims.quote: So, if you look at my pieces of content here that are photos, you'll see this one 150 bucks.

claims.claim: A Costco photo post earned $110.
claims.quote: This one about Costco, 110 bucks.

claims.claim: A sober-living housing photo post earned $102.
claims.quote: This one about sober living housing, $102.

claims.claim: A sport-courts photo post earned $80.
claims.quote: Sport courts, $80. This was about posting about the donuts that I ate in Alabama, $70.

claims.claim: A post about donuts he ate in Alabama earned $70.
claims.quote: Sport courts, $80. This was about posting about the donuts that I ate in Alabama, $70.

claims.claim: He says the examples add up to tens of thousands of dollars per month.
claims.quote: And it adds up to tens of thousands of dollars a month.

claims.claim: He says each Instagram account can have four other subaccounts.
claims.quote: Every single Instagram account can have four other sub accounts under it.

claims.claim: He cites eight billion people as the potential audience for niche content.
claims.quote: I don't care who you are or where you live, you have a very unique insight into something that other people in the world would find interesting because there's 8 billion of us

claims.claim: He says viral business videos typically get 500,000 to 5 million views, while 12–15 million views is rare in that niche.
claims.quote: For the business niche, you really never get over 12 to 15 million, and those are rare. A viral business video is going to have 500,000 to 5 million typically.

claims.claim: He says his short-form videos earn about $0.25 per 1,000 views, roughly the same as his YouTube short-form rate.
claims.quote: So I get paid about 25 cents per thousand views on my short form videos, which is pretty high. And it's about the same as what I make on YouTube for my short form videos.

claims.claim: He recommends keeping a scripted short video to about 60 seconds.
claims.quote: Give it a good hook. I need a retention hack in there to keep people watching to the end. And I don't want it to be any more than 60 seconds.

claims.claim: He says he needed his first 50 or 100 videos to learn how to edit out pauses.
claims.quote: Even I didn't even know how to edit out pauses for like my first 50 or 100 videos. So, I just kept retaking videos until I got it all right in one take.

claims.claim: He says a new account with zero followers may initially reach only a couple hundred people.
claims.quote: Now, keep in mind if you have zero followers on Facebook, you started a brand new account, this is going to be shown to very few people, couple hundred people. It takes time.

claims.claim: Recent posts took five to ten minutes to make, and he paid an editor about $10 to edit them.
claims.quote: It took me 5 to 10 minutes to make. I paid an editor about $10 to edit it.

claims.claim: He says those edited posts earned $500–$2,000 each.
claims.quote: And they made me $500 to $2,000 each.

acquisition_channels.details: He publishes original commentary and other content natively across Facebook, Instagram, YouTube Shorts, Snapchat Spotlight, Twitter, Threads, and LinkedIn; he also sources inspiration from Instagram and Twitter.

ideas.delivery: The creator finds content, adds commentary or analysis, records or creates a post, edits it, and uploads it to social platforms. He describes using AI tools for idea generation and scripts, while the creator supplies the insight and handles publishing.
ideas.other_uk_rules: UK copyright law uses fair dealing exceptions rather than a general US-style fair use doctrine; the transcript does not establish that this reuse would qualify under UK law. Get UK-specific permission or legal advice before relying on commentary or repurposing exceptions.

idea.name: Junk removal service
idea.one_liner: Remove household junk for paying customers, starting with rented vehicles and scaling to a truck as demand grows.
idea.customer: Households or property owners needing unwanted items removed.
idea.offer: Collect and haul away junk, charging by time or job.
idea.revenue_model: Service fees; the speaker suggests an hourly rate and gives rough rental, revenue, and margin figures.

key_quotes.quote: Step one would be find a paying customer.
There is no reason to buy a dump truck right off the bat.
But the profit margins on this business can range between 10 and 35%.

claims.claim: A woman in a video reportedly grew a junk-removal business to $150,000 in six months.
claims.quote: It's a woman talking about how she grew her junk removal business to $150,000 in 6 months.

claims.claim: The example business was described as doing three jobs a day, five days a week, and $150,000 in six months.
claims.quote: So, three jobs a day, 5 days a week, 150,000 in 6 months, buy a dump truck.

claims.claim: He says the referenced $150,000 was revenue, not profit.
claims.quote: The screenshot shows it's 150,000 in profit, but that's not profit. That's revenue.

claims.claim: A new operator could probably find two or three customers by posting to a personal Facebook account.
claims.quote: You could probably post to your personal Facebook account and find two or three customers right off the bat.

claims.claim: He suggests charging about $50 per hour per person.
claims.quote: Call it 50 bucks an hour per person. That's about what a mover would charge as well.

claims.claim: At 40 hours a week and that rate, he estimates $100,000 a year.
claims.quote: And at 40 hours a week, that's $100,000 a year. So, not bad.

claims.claim: He suggests renting a 26-foot truck rather than buying one at the outset.
claims.quote: You're going to rent a 26-footer just like this.

claims.claim: He estimates the truck rental at about $40 per day plus $0.75 per mile.
claims.quote: It's going to cost you about 40 bucks a day plus 75 cents per mile.

claims.claim: He says two young operators he interviewed make over $1 million a year.
claims.quote: Today, they're making over a million bucks a year.

claims.claim: He would wait until about $20,000 monthly revenue before buying his first truck.
claims.quote: And I wouldn't buy my first truck until I'm at about $20,000 a month in revenue.

claims.claim: He says profit margins can range from 10% to 35%.
claims.quote: But the profit margins on this business can range between 10 and 35%.

acquisition_channels.details: He suggests posting on a personal Facebook account to find initial customers.
He says Facebook ads and Google ads are options.
He says SEO is also an option.

ideas.delivery: The operator collects and hauls away customers' junk, initially renting a U-Haul truck and later potentially buying a truck as revenue grows.

prices: about $40 per day plus $0.75 per mile for a 26-foot rental truck
about $20,000 monthly revenue before buying a truck

ideas.other_uk_rules: UK waste carrier registration and waste duty-of-care requirements may apply; the transcript does not discuss them.

idea.name: Long-form YouTube videos

idea.customer: YouTube viewers and advertisers reached through the videos.
idea.revenue_model: YouTube monetization; the speaker reports net revenue per thousand views.

key_quotes.quote: It's shockingly easy to make a very nice living creating long- form YouTube videos like six figures plus.
After months or years of testing and you find the format that works for you, YouTube can be very profitable, but it is a ton of work to get there.

claims.claim: The speaker says his long-form YouTube videos earn about $17 net per 1,000 views, around 60 times his short-form rate.
claims.quote: Now for my long form videos on YouTube, I make about 60 times that. I make about $17 net to me per thousand long form views on YouTube.

claims.claim: He says finding a profitable YouTube format can take months or years of testing.
claims.quote: After months or years of testing and you find the format that works for you, YouTube can be very profitable, but it is a ton of work to get there.

claims.claim: He states that he makes money on YouTube.
claims.quote: I do make money on YouTube and I have a hard stance that I can say in good conscience is true.

acquisition_channels.details: Publish long-form videos on YouTube; no specific audience acquisition tactics are given.

ideas.delivery: The creator makes and publishes long-form videos on YouTube; the speaker describes testing formats over months or years.

idea.name: Grow a newsletter from Facebook traffic
idea.one_liner: Send social followers to a landing page to join an owned email audience, then earn referral payments through SparkLoop.
idea.customer: Facebook followers who opt into the newsletter; its subject and reader profile are not stated.
idea.offer: A newsletter and an owned email audience built from social traffic.
idea.revenue_model: SparkLoop payments of $0.50–$5 per email; other newsletter monetization is not stated.

key_quotes.quote: And you're going to link to it in the top of your comment on every single post, every reel, everything you post to Facebook.
And Spark Loop will pay you between 50 cents and $5 for every single email.

claims.claim: He says driving Facebook traffic off-platform to acquire email addresses can make more money.
claims.quote: And if you stick around to the end, I will show you how you can make way, way, way more money by driving that Facebook traffic off of Facebook.

claims.claim: He says SparkLoop pays between $0.50 and $5 for each email.
claims.quote: And Spark Loop will pay you between 50 cents and $5 for every single email.

claims.claim: He says his newsletter grew from 96,000 to 250,000 subscribers in 12 months.
claims.quote: I mean, just look at how much my newsletter has grown over the last 12 months. From 96,000 subscribers to 250,000.

claims.claim: He says almost all the growth was organic and most of that came from the link under Facebook posts.
claims.quote: And almost all of that was organic growth. And most of that organic growth all came from that one link under every single Facebook post.

claims.claim: He says Facebook pays him to move its users off Facebook.
claims.quote: So, Facebook is paying me to take their users off of Facebook.

acquisition_channels.details: He links a landing page in the comments on every Facebook post and reel to direct followers to the newsletter.

ideas.delivery: Create a landing page with Carrd or Beehive, link it from Facebook posts, and collect email subscribers for a newsletter; SparkLoop pays per email according to the speaker.
ideas.other_uk_rules: UK GDPR and PECR apply to collecting email addresses and sending marketing emails; provide appropriate privacy information and consent or other valid basis, plus an unsubscribe route. If selling paid subscriptions, DMCC Act subscription rules may apply; paid subscriptions are not stated here.
